items.followUp: What role do chloroplasts play in plant cells?

rubric.why: Checks the pigments and the plant parts whose colours they produce.
rubric.description: Chromoplasts contain pigments that give colour to flowers and fruits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chromoplast pigments colour flowers and/or fruits (both are not required).

rubric.why: Checks the biological importance of the colours produced by chromoplasts.
rubric.description: These colours can attract pollinators or animals that disperse seeds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking colour to attracting pollinators or seed-dispersing animals.

modelAnswer: Chromoplasts contain pigments that give colour to flowers and fruits.
These colours help attract pollinators and animals that disperse seeds.

items.followUp: State two functions of leucoplasts in plant cells.

rubric.why: Checks the basic cellular organisation of protists.
rubric.description: Protists are eukaryotic organisms and are mostly unicellular.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that protists are eukaryotic or mostly unicellular.

rubric.why: Checks recognition of the main groups of protists.
rubric.description: They include plant-like algae, animal-like protozoa, and fungus-like protists.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming at least two groups or describing the plant-like and animal-like types.

modelAnswer: Protists are eukaryotic organisms and are mostly unicellular.
They include plant-like algae, animal-like protozoa, and fungus-like protists.

items.followUp: Write the scientific names of mango and housefly.

rubric.why: Checks the scientific name of onion.
rubric.description: The scientific name of onion is Allium cepa.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct binomial name of onion.

rubric.why: Checks the scientific name used for sea star.
rubric.description: The scientific name of sea star is Asterias rubens.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Asterias rubens; accept Asterias as the genus if the species is omitted.

items.followUp: State two ways mitosis is important in multicellular organisms.

rubric.why: Checks mitosis as a means of increasing cell number.
rubric.description: Mitosis enables growth by increasing the number of cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying growth or an increase in cell number.

rubric.why: Checks another recognised significance of mitosis.
rubric.description: Mitosis repairs or replaces cells, supports asexual reproduction, and maintains chromosome number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one additional correct significance.

modelAnswer: Mitosis increases the number of cells and enables growth.
It repairs or replaces damaged cells; it also supports asexual reproduction and maintains chromosome number.

items.followUp: Draw and label an anaphase stage of mitosis.

rubric.why: Checks that the drawing represents cytokinesis rather than another mitotic stage.
rubric.description: Draw a cell dividing its cytoplasm, showing a cleavage furrow in an animal cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a recognisable dividing cell with a furrow (or a plant-cell plate).

rubric.why: Checks the essential labels and the resulting daughter cells.
rubric.description: Label the daughter nuclei and the cleavage furrow (or cell plate in a plant cell).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly labelling the main cytokinesis structures.

modelAnswer: Draw an oval animal cell 6 cm wide and 4 cm high.
Draw two round daughter nuclei, each 0.8 cm in diameter, inside the cell near opposite ends.
Draw the cell membrane pinching inward at the middle to form a cleavage furrow, showing the cytoplasm dividing.
Label the cell membrane, cleavage furrow, and daughter nuclei.

items.followUp: Name the site of glycolysis and the site of the Krebs cycle.

rubric.why: Checks one of the main stages of aerobic respiration.
rubric.description: The first main stage is glycolysis.

rubric.why: Checks the other main stage expected in the textbook treatment.
rubric.description: The second main stage is the Krebs cycle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle).

modelAnswer: The two main stages of aerobic respiration are glycolysis and the Krebs cycle.

items.followUp: Explain how an enzyme's active site binds its substrate.

rubric.why: Checks the shape-specific binding principle of the model.
rubric.description: The enzyme's active site has a shape complementary to its specific substrate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the substrate fits the enzyme's specifically shaped active site.

rubric.why: Checks the lock-and-key comparison and/or its outcome.
rubric.description: The substrate fits like a key in a lock, forming an enzyme-substrate complex; products are then released.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the lock-and-key comparison or for stating that the complex forms and products are released.

modelAnswer: In the lock-and-key model, an enzyme's active site has a specific shape complementary to its substrate.
The substrate fits into the active site like a key fits a lock, forming an enzyme-substrate complex; products are then released.

items.followUp: What is an inorganic cofactor? Give one example.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of a cofactor.
rubric.description: A cofactor is a non-protein component required for an enzyme to function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a cofactor as a non-protein component required for enzyme activity.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of a coenzyme as an organic helper molecule.
rubric.description: A coenzyme is an organic non-protein molecule that assists an enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a coenzyme as an organic molecule that assists enzyme action.

modelAnswer: A cofactor is a non-protein component required for an enzyme to function; it may be an inorganic ion or an organic molecule.
A coenzyme is an organic non-protein molecule that assists an enzyme in its activity.
